description_full: Penske Automotive Group, Inc., a diversified transportation services company, operates automotive and commercial truck dealerships in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and internationally. It operates through four segments: Retail Automotive, Retail Commercial Truck, Other, and Non-Automotive Investments. The company operates franchise dealerships under franchise agreements with various automotive manufacturers and distributors. It is also involved in the sale of new and used vehicles, maintenance and repair services, sale and placement of third-party finance and insurance products, third-party extended service and maintenance contracts, replacement and aftermarket automotive products, collision repair services, and wholesale of parts. In addition, the company operates a heavy and medium duty truck dealership, which offers Freightliner and Western Star branded trucks, as well as offers a range of used trucks. Further, it imports and distributes Western Star heavy-duty trucks, MAN heavy and medium duty trucks and buses, and Dennis Eagle refuse collection vehicles with associated parts, as well as distributes diesel and gas engines, and power systems. Penske Automotive Group, Inc. was incorporated in 1990 and is headquartered in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan. Penske Automotive Group, Inc. operates as a subsidiary of Penske Corporation, Inc.

financial_summary: Penske Automotive Group, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $13.9B market cap on $31.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 9% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 15% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $650M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 4.7×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 21% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 26% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 7% below the high.

About $79.3M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.7x its yearly average volume.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $162 (margin of safety -31%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 12%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $128 to $207 (P10-P90).
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Cyclical peers: cheaper on P/E 14.8 vs 18.8, richer on EV/EBITDA 16.6 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 21.4 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 137% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $211 on average, 1% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 8.6% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.24).
It runs a 15% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.04x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.2x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($64.7M of cash against $2.2B of debt), with interest covered 4.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.2, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.99 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.6% over 3 years, 9.2% over 5 years and 5.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 66% of profits supports about 11.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -8.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.9x depreciation (1.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 21.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 77%.
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 2.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 38.2% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 12.4% of the float, 3.3 days to cover.
people: With about 28,900 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 2.9x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 7.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $23K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $2.8M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
